en: May Sarasvatī, who is entirely white, the female swan in the forest of the lotus-faces of the four-faced Brahmā, delight forever in my mind. (Kāvyādarśa 1.1)
Having condensed the earlier treatises and observed actual literary practices,
we compose these characteristics of poetry according to our own ability.
In this world, the course of worldly affairs proceeds entirely through the grace of speech alone— both that of those who have been instructed by the learned and that of the learned themselves.
This entire triple world would become total darkness if the light of the Word did not shine throughout the duration of saṃsāra. (DKD 1.4)
Having obtained the mirror of literature—the reflection of the glory of the first king—his fame does not perish of its own accord even in their absence; behold! 1.5.
The wise remember that the word "cow" (gauḥ), when properly employed, is a cow that milks all desires;
yet, when wrongly employed, that very same word proclaims the "cowness" of the speaker.
Therefore, not even a slight defect in poetry should ever be overlooked;
for even a beautiful body becomes unsightly by a single case of leprosy.
How can a person who does not know the scriptures distinguish between virtues and faults?
Does a blind man have the capacity to perceive differences in form? (DKD 1.8)
Therefore, with the aim of facilitating the linguistic proficiency of living beings, the wise have composed the rules for the formation of words through speech that follows diverse paths.
By them, both the body and the ornaments of poems have been shown.
First, the body is a sequence of words delimited by a desired meaning.
That [prose composition] is established as being of three kinds: verse, prose, and mixed.
Verse consists of four lines, and it is of two types: *vṛtta* (metrical) and *jāti* (quantitative).
In the *Chandoviciti*, the entire expansion of that [prosody] has been demonstrated;
that science is a boat for those wishing to enter the deep ocean of poetry. (DKD 1.12)

The *muktaka*, *kulaka*, *koṣa*, and *saṃghāta*— such are the types of extensive poetic compositions (*padyavistara*) that are not explicitly mentioned [in the formal definitions], because they are merely constituent parts of a *sargabandha*.
A composition in cantos is called a *mahākāvya* (great poem); its definition is as follows:
its opening consists of a benediction, a salutation, or an indication of the subject matter. (DK 1.14)
Whether derived from historical narratives or otherwise, it should always have a virtuous basis,
be directed toward the fruit of the four aims of human life, and feature a noble hero.
By means of descriptions of cities, oceans, mountains, the seasons, and the rising of the moon and sun;
and by means of garden parties, water-sports, drinking bouts, and festivals of pleasure.
Through separations and marriages, descriptions of the birth of princes, as well as through counsel, the dispatch of envoys, expeditions, sacrifices, and the triumphs of heroes; DKd 1.17.
It is adorned, not condensed, filled continuously with aesthetic flavors and emotional states,
composed of cantos that are not overly extensive, written in melodious meters, and joined by well-constructed transitions.
A poem that delights the world, endowed everywhere with diverse narratives and possessed of true ornamentation, becomes enduring for the duration of an eon. (DKD 1.19)

Even if it lacks some of these constituent parts, a poem is not thereby flawed, provided that there is perfection in those elements that have been employed, which satisfies those who know the craft. (1.20)
Having first presented the protagonist by way of his virtues, the subsequent refutation of his enemies— this is a path that is naturally beautiful.
Describing even an enemy’s lineage, valor, learning, and so forth, and then proclaiming the hero’s excellence through his victory over him—this delights us. (DKD 1.22)
A continuous sequence of words without metrical feet is prose (*gadya*), which has two divisions: the *ākhyāyikā* and the *kathā*.
Of these two, it is said that the *ākhyāyikā* is as follows.
Whether these words are spoken by the protagonist himself or by another, there is no fault here in the manifestation of one's own virtues, for they proclaim the actual state of affairs. (DKD 1.24)
Moreover, an absence of restriction is observed there as well, because it is prompted by others;
whether the speaker is someone else or oneself, what indeed could be the distinguishing cause (or characteristic)?

The *vaktra* (introductory verse), the *aparavaktra*, and the presence of breath-like pauses (*socchvāsatva*) are the distinguishing marks of an *ākhyāyikā*; these may also occur incidentally in *kathās*.
Why is there no entry [into the definition of *āryā*] for *vaktra* and *aparavaktra* as there is for *āryā* and others?
Furthermore, since divisions such as *lambha* and so forth are observed, what is the point of mentioning "breath" (*ucchvāsa*) as a formal element (*vastu*)? (DK 1.27)
Thus, the *jāti* (class of composition) is said to be designated by two names: *kathā* and *ākhyāyikā*; all other remaining types of narrative (*ākhyāna-jāti*) will be included within these very two.
The abduction of a maiden, battle, separation, and the rise of prosperity—these are no different from the [episodes] found in epic compositions; they are not indeed distinctive merits.
The mark produced by a poet’s creative genius does not become faulty even when applied elsewhere;
for what indeed cannot be achieved by those who have mastered themselves in the accomplishment of their desired goals? (DK 1.30)
Dramas and other such works are mixed compositions; their detailed treatment is found elsewhere.
A certain type consisting of both prose and verse is designated as *campū*.
Furthermore, the noble ones say that this literature consisting of speech is fourfold: Sanskrit, Prākṛta, Apabhraṃśa, and the mixed. (DKD 1.32)
That which is called *saṃskṛta* is the divine speech expounded by the great seers;
its derivatives (*tadbhava*), its equals (*tatsama*), and the regional (*deśī*)—these constitute the manifold system of *prākṛta*.
They know the language based on Mahārāṣṭra as the most excellent Prākṛt;
it is the ocean of jewels of well-spoken verses, wherein such works as the Setubandha are composed.
Śaurasenī, Gauḍī, Lāṭī, and other similar varieties are thus included under the term "Prākṛta" in common usage.
The speech of Ābhīras and others is known as *apabhraṃśa* in poetic works;
in the technical treatises (*śāstra*), however, anything other than *saṃskṛta* is declared to be *apabhraṃśa*.
Sanskrit consists of works such as the *sargabandha*; Prākṛt consists of works such as the *skandhaka*;
Apabhraṃśa consists of works such as the *osara*; and the mixed style consists of works such as the *nāṭaka*.
For this narrative is composed in all languages and in Sanskrit;
they call the Bṛhatkathā, which consists of the Bhūtabhāṣā, a work of wondrous meaning.
Lāsya, cchalita, śampā, and so forth are for the purpose of being seen, whereas the other is only for being heard; thus, this twofold path has also been described.
There are many paths of speech with subtle differences from one another;
among them, the Vaidarbha and Gauḍīya styles are described as having clearly distinct characteristics.
Cohesion, clarity, evenness, sweetness, gentleness, explicitness of meaning, loftiness, vigor, luster, and concentration. (DKD 1.41)
Thus, these ten qualities are remembered as the life-breaths of the Vaidarbha style;
their opposite is generally observed in the Gauḍa path.
"Coalescent" (śliṣṭa) is that which lacks looseness and consists primarily of vowels with little breath-force, such as a garland of *mālatī* flowers thick with swarms of restless bees. (DKD 1.43)
The Gauḍas favor that [ornament] because of its weightiness of composition, regarding it as *anuprāsa* (alliteration);
whereas the Vaidarbhas consider it like a jasmine garland trampled by bees.
"Like the moon, the spot, possessing the luster of a blue lotus, extends its splendor"—this statement is fortunate in its clarity, for its meaning is well-established and evident. (DKD 1.45)

The Gauḍīyas do not accept even that which is "understood" (vyutpanna) if it is not well-established [in usage], as for example: "the pale moon, whose mark resembles a lotus that is not excessively white. (DK 1.46)
Your poetic compositions are uniform and free from unevenness; their structures consist of soft, clear, and middling syllables, arising from the arrangement of sounds that are soft, clear, or mixed.
The Malaya breeze, made eloquent by the warbling of cuckoos and sprinkled with clear droplets from the water of leaping spray-covered cascades, comes toward me.
The gentle Malaya breeze, fragrant with the scent of sandalwood,
vies with the breath from the mouths of beautiful women who have restrained their fortitude.
Thus, disregarding the disparity between these two— the meaning and the ornaments—
and paying heed only to the latter, the eastern tradition of poetry flourished.
His speech is sweet and full of flavor, and even in its subject matter there resides a state of aesthetic relish (rasa),
by which the wise are intoxicated, just as honey-bees are by honey.
Whatever commonality is experienced through any given phoneme, that proximity of words possessing such a form constitutes alliteration, which brings forth aesthetic flavor (*rasa*). (DKD 1.52)
From the moment this king, who was beloved by the Brahmins, attained royal fortune,
there has been a festival of Dharma in this world ever since.
Thus, this [poetic figure] is not esteemed by the Gauḍas, for alliteration is their favorite;
yet even more than alliteration, this [poetic figure] is generally desired by the Vaidarbhas.

Alliteration (*anuprāsa*) is the repetition of phonemes both within verses and within words, provided there is proximity that awakens the latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) of prior experience. (DK 1.55)
Upon the moon— the crest-ornament of the autumn night and possessing the splendor of a cluster of kunda flowers— the dark spot bears the beauty of a bee, resembling a sapphire.
"O timid one, behold this lovely lunar orb in the sky;
it is intent on mercilessly slaying my mind, which is already overcome by passion."
Thus, they desire alliteration with an interval that is not too distant,
but not [in a case] such as "The moon is like the lotus-face of Rāmā."
Love is harsh, the beloved is wicked, and our bodies and anger have grown thin; pride has vanished, passion has increased, delusion has arisen, and our vital breaths have departed.
Thus, [the southerners] avoid harshness and looseness of construction;
therefore, the Southerners do not employ alliteration in this manner.
The wise know that *yamaka* consists of the repetition of syllable-groups;
however, because it is not exclusively sweet, it will be treated later.
Granted that every ornament sprinkles flavor upon the meaning, nevertheless,
it is non-vulgarity alone that bears this burden for the most part.
"O maiden, why do you not desire me who desires you?"— this vulgar pursuit of worldly interests leads only to bitterness.
"O fair-eyed one, it is true that the outcaste Kandarpa is merciless toward me;
yet, by good fortune, he is free from envy toward you. Such is the meaning of the first line, which brings forth aesthetic flavor.
Even in the case of sound, vulgarity certainly exists due to the mention of what is unfit for polite society,
as for example the word beginning with the letter *ya* when describing a festival of love.
Furthermore, that which causes a faulty understanding—either through the connection of words or through the meaning of the sentence—is *grāmya* (vulgar), as in: "She who is your beloved. (DKd 1.66)
"A man of vigor, having struck hard, is rested"—
such sayings as these they do not praise in either of the two paths.
The use of terms such as *bhaginī* (sister) and *bhagavatī* (venerable lady) everywhere is approved;
this is called "sweetness" (*mādhurya*), which is [the quality of] delicacy (*sukumāratā*).
In this [poetic style], what consists mostly of non-harsh syllables is desired as "delicate" (sukumāra);
yet, the fault of looseness in composition is also shown when everything is delicate.
Having fanned their tails into circles, the peacocks dance with sweet songs from their throats at this time when the sky is garlanded with clouds.
Thus, even a meaning that is not particularly forceful, nor an ornament of such a kind,
ascends to the minds of the wise solely by virtue of its delicacy.
"Blazing," so others say; by its abundance, even that which is difficult to restrain is bound.
"In an instant, the faction of the Kṣatriyas has been utterly destroyed"—thus [it was said]. (DKd 1.72)

The clarity of meaning and the impossibility of misinterpretation regarding the sense are [illustrated] by the verse: "The earth was lifted from the ocean, which had been reddened by the blood of serpents trampled by his hooves. (DK 1.73)
"The earth was lifted from the red ocean by the Great Boar"— when only this much is stated, the fact that [the earth] was blood-red from the serpent's blood remains to be inferred.
One does not hold such [a view] in high regard for either of these two paths;
for a cognition that transgresses the principles of words and logic is not beautiful.
When some quality characterized by excellence is perceived upon its mention, that is called the "Sublime" (udāra); by this, the path of poetry is graced.
O Lord, the piteous gaze of supplicants, having fallen but once upon your face, remains in that very state and never looks upon the face of another.
Thus, in this statement regarding renunciation, its excellence is clearly perceived;
by this very path, other matters governed by the same logic should be inferred.
Some maintain that [the name] should be noble and endowed with praiseworthy epithets, such as *Līlāmbuja*, *Krīḍāsara*, *Hemāṅgada*, and so forth. (DKD 1.79)
Abundance of compounds constitutes the vitality of prose;
even in verse, this alone is the ultimate resort for those of the non-South (the Easterners).
Through the combination of many or few heavy and light syllables,
that visible form appears in various high and low varieties within narratives and other literary works.
With the entire bed of sunbeams scattered across the summit of the setting mountain,
the western quarter appeared like a woman wearing a crimson garment upon her full breasts.
Thus, even in verse, the Easterners compose speech that is forceful (*ojasvinī*);
others, however, desire a forcefulness of words that is unconfused and pleasing to the heart, as follows: (DKD 1.83).
Whose mind, already afflicted by desire, will not be further inflamed by a woman whose saffron-dyed garment clings to the slopes of her breasts like the glow of twilight?
It is beloved by the entire world because it transcends worldly concerns;
and this is seen even in descriptions within the accounts of worldly affairs.
Those alone are truly called "homes" which a mass of asceticism such as yours honors with the purifying dust of your feet.
O lady of faultless limbs, as these two breasts of yours expand, there is no sufficient space within the interval of your vine-like arms.
Thus, this very thing, when refined by the narration of particulars, becomes pleasing to everyone who follows the ways of the world.
When a meaning intended for expression is superimposed to such an extreme degree that it seems as if transcending the world, the wise are exceedingly delighted by it, but other people are not.
From this day forward, our home shall be worthy of veneration like the abode of a god,
its every impurity washed away by the falling dust of your feet.
The Creator, failing to perceive that the space allotted for your breasts would expand in such a manner, fashioned it far too small.
This has been called "hyperbole" (atyukti); this is the method cherished by the Gauḍas, whereas that previously set forth belongs to the essence of another path.
When one correctly applies another dharma elsewhere, in accordance with worldly conventions, that is considered "samādhi" (concentration), as it has been taught.
"The night-lotuses close and the day-lotuses open"—thus, through the superimposition of the activity of eyes, the word denoting them is obtained. (DK 1.94)
Expressions such as "spit out," "vomited," or "regurgitated" rely on metaphorical usage;
while they may be exceedingly beautiful in one context, elsewhere they plunge into the realm of vulgarity.
The lotuses, having drunk the sparks of fire spat out by the rays of the sun,
seem to vomit them back again through their mouths, which have disgorged ruddy pollen.
Thus, as it is said: "The bride spits out what was once dear as 'not dear,'" so too is the simultaneous superimposition (adhyāsa) of multiple attributes traditionally taught.
Exhausted by the heavy burden of their wombs, these rows of clouds, thundering,
now rest upon the laps of the mountain plateaus.
Sleeping on a friend’s lap, heaving sighs, heaviness, and exhaustion—
these many symptoms of pregnancy are displayed here.
This very quality called *samādhi* is the essence of poetry; the entire community of poets follows it alone. (DKD 1.100)
Thus, these two paths are distinct based on the definition of their essential natures;
however, it is impossible to state all their subdivisions as they exist among individual poets.
There is a vast difference between the sweetness of sugarcane, milk, molasses, and so forth;
yet even Sarasvatī herself would not be able to describe it.
Innate genius, extensive and stainless learning, and unremitting application— these are the causes of excellence in poetry.

Even if there exists no marvelous intuition that follows upon the qualities of former predispositions, speech that has been cultivated through learning and effort certainly bestows some grace. (DKD 1.104)
Therefore, those who desire fame must indeed worship Sarasvatī incessantly and without weariness;
for even when their poetic talent is meager, people who have exerted effort in it are able to move within the assemblies of the wise.
Thus ends the first chapter, titled "The Classification of Styles," in the *Kāvyādarśa* composed by Ācārya Daṇḍin.
They declare that the factors which produce the beauty of poetry are the ornaments (*alaṃkāra*); yet even now they are being variously conceptualized—who could describe them in their entirety? (2.1)
However, the seed of conceptual constructions has been demonstrated by previous masters; this effort of ours is merely to refine that very seed.
Some ornaments have already been mentioned previously for the purpose of classifying the paths; now, another common collection of ornaments is being demonstrated.

Description of intrinsic nature (svabhāvākhyāna), simile (upamā), metaphor (rūpaka), the lamp-ornament (dīpaka) and repetition (āvṛtti), the parable (ākṣepa), the corroboration by another matter (arthāntaranyāsa), contrast (vyatireka), and the description of the causeless (vibhāvanā). DKD 2.4.

Conciseness (samāsa), hyperbole (atiśaya), poetic fancy (utprekṣā), cause (hetu), the subtle (sūkṣma), the minute (lava), sequence (krama), the lovely (preyaḥ), the sentiment-filled (rasavat), the forceful (ūrjasvin), the periphrastic (paryāyokta), and the composed (samāhita). 2.5.
Hyperbole, concealment, paronomasia, particularity, equal pairing, contradiction, praise of the irrelevant, indirect praise, and illustration; DK 2.6.
Co-expression (sahokti), exchange (parivṛtti), benediction (āśis), and the intermingled (saṃkīrṇa), as well as the manifest (bhāvika)—
thus have the ornaments of speech been shown by the ancient masters.
Directly revealing the various states of the forms of things, it is an ornament such as *svabhāvokti* (description of nature), *jāti* (generalization), and so forth, as follows: [DKD 2.8]
With beaks that are copper-red and curved, wings that are tenderly green,
and throats marked with three-colored stripes— these parrots possess sweet voices.
With his eyes rolling and his throat filled with cooing, the pigeon,
desiring to dally, circles about and kisses his beloved.
Causing horripilation to arise on the limbs, producing bliss in the mind, and causing the eyes to close— this touch of the beloved proceeds.
With blackness around his throat, holding a skull-cup in his hand, and crowned by the moon,
the bull-bannered god appeared with matted locks of glossy copper-brown hue.
Such is the description of genus, action, quality, substance, and essential nature;
it holds sovereign sway over the treatises, and it is likewise desired in poetry.
Wherever a semblance of similarity is perceived in any way whatsoever, that is called "simile" (upamā); its various elaborations are now demonstrated.
"O charming one, your palm is like a copper-colored lotus"—this is a direct simile of quality (*dharmopamā*), because it explicitly demonstrates a common attribute. (DKD 2.15)
"Your face is like a lotus, and your eyes are like blue lotuses"—
this is indeed a *vastūpamā*, as it is perceived as having a single common attribute.
"The lotus has become as if blooming like your face"—
this is considered a "reversal simile" (viparyāsopamā) due to the inversion of common renown.
"Your face is like a lotus, and a lotus is like your face"—
this is a mutual simile (anyonyopamā), proclaiming the excellence of each over the other.
"Your face is equal only to the lotus, and not to anything else"—
this is *niyamopamā* (restricted simile), because it excludes comparison with other things.
"The lotus follows after your face, and there is another such [thing] as well;
if it exists, let it be its maker"—this is an unrestricted simile (aniyamopamā).
There is also the cumulative simile (*samuccayopamā*), such as this: "Your face does not equal the moon by its beauty alone, but also by its function known as 'gladdening'."
Your face is seen in you alone, while the moon is seen in the sky;
there is only this much difference and no other—this is *atiśayopamā* (hyperbolic simile).
"The glory of her face resides in me alone"—enough with such boasting by the moon!
Since that same glory exists in the lotus as well, this is an "imagined simile" (utprekṣitopamā).
"If there were some lotus with wandering eyes, O fair-browed one,
may it bear the splendor of your face"— this is a marvelous simile (adbhutopamā).
"O slender-limbed one, having imagined your face to be the moon, I pursue even the moon with the hope that it is your face"— this is remembered as the simile of delusion (*mohopamā*).
"Is this a lotus with bees wandering within, or is it your face with its tremulous eyes? My mind wavers"—this is the simile of doubt (*saṃśayopamā*).
"The luster of the lotus, which is eclipsed by the moon, does not cause shame to the moon;
therefore, this is indeed your face"—this is "determinative simile" (nirṇayopamā).
"Your face is like a lotus— glorious, fragrant, and rivaling the cool-rayed moon"— this is known as a paronomastic simile (śleṣopamā).
Because it is expressed by words that possess the same form, that is "Equal Simile" (*samānopamā*), as for example:
"This row of clouds in the garden is like a young girl, beautifying the grove of *sāla* trees."
"The lotus has much pollen and the moon wanes; though your face is similar to these two, it is superior"—this is known as a "contemptuous simile" (nindopamā).
"The lotus from which even Brahmā arises, and the moon borne upon the head of Śambhu—these two are equal to your face. This is called praise-comparison (praśaṃsopamā).
"My mind desires to declare that your face is equal to the moon;
let that be either a merit or a fault"—this they know as *ācikhyāsopamā* (the simile of the desire to declare).
"The hundred-petaled lotus," "the autumnal moon," and "your face"—these three are mutually contradictory; this is considered *virodhopamā* (contradictory simile).
"The moon, being stained and dull-witted, can never rival your face"— this is indeed a simile of negation (pratiṣedhopamā).
"Your face is marked by deer-like eyes, while the moon is marked by a deer; yet even so, the moon is merely equal [to your face] and does not surpass it"—this is a flattering simile (*caṭūpamā*).

"This is not a lotus; this is indeed a face. These are not two bees; these are the eyes"—because the similarity is so clearly evident, that is merely a comparison stating the actual fact (*tattvākhyānopamā*).
"Your face, having surpassed the beauty of both the moon and the lotus,
became equal to itself"— this is the "uncommon simile" (asādhāraṇopamā).
"Your face shines as if the essence of the radiance of all lotuses were gathered together somewhere"— this they know to be an *abhūtopamā* (a hyperbolic simile).
"Poison from the moon's orb, fire from sandalwood, or harsh speech from this mouth"—this is an impossible simile (*asaṃbhāvitopamā*). (DKD 2.39)
"Your touch is as cool as sandalwood water, moonbeams, moonstones, and the like"— through these many similes, they make known its extraordinary quality.
"O slender-limbed one, your face is as if carved out from the orb of the moon or extracted from the heart of a lotus"— this is *vikriyopamā* (metaphor by transformation).
"Vigor bestowed beauty upon you, as sunlight does upon the day, as the sun does upon the sky, and as the day does upon the firmament"—
this is considered a "garland simile" (mālopamā).

If a certain meaning of a sentence is compared with another meaning of a sentence, that is the simile of the meaning of a sentence (*vākyārthopamā*); it is of two kinds, depending on whether there is one or more instances of the word *iva*.
Your face, with its tremulous eyes and the radiance of visible teeth, shines like a lotus with hovering bees and faintly visible filaments.
Like a bee repeatedly drinking from a lotus, I took my pleasure by gazing again and again at the face of that slender-limbed woman, which was like a lotus upon a lotus-pond.

Having introduced some subject matter, the presentation of another thing possessing a similar quality results in the perception of a likeness; this is *prativastūpamā* (simile by parallelism), as for example: [DKD 2.46].
Not even one like you has been born among the kings being born even today;
indeed, there is no second tree of the *pārijāta*!

When, for the sake of performing a single action, one equalizes the inferior by means of the superior, that which they express is known as the simile of equal conjunction (*tulyayogopamā*), as follows: // DKD 2.48 //
Puloman was the guardian of heaven for its protection, while you are the protector of the earth;
by him the Asuras were slain, and by you, arrogant kings are destroyed.
"O King, you emulate the moon in beauty, the sun in splendor, and the ocean in steadfastness"— this is considered a simile based on a cause (hetūpamā).
Neither a difference in gender or number, nor even a disparity in degree,
is sufficient to vitiate a simile, provided that it causes no distress to the wise.
This eunuch walks like a woman; she speaks like a man; this one is as dear to me as my own life; and this knowledge is acquired by me like wealth. (DKD 2.52)
O protector of the earth, like you the king of the gods shines resplendent; O monarch, by your splendor you are fully capable of ascending to the rank of the sun.
In such cases as these, charm is never indeed abandoned;
yet there is always some degree of agitation, just as occurs in the performance of those skilled in speech.
The moon is white like a female swan; the sky is stainless like lakes;
a soldier devoted to his master is like a dog; and a firefly shines like the sun.
Such things are avoided by the virtuous; let the wise themselves consider the reason for this in order to discern its merits and faults.
The words *iva*, *vat*, *vā*, *yathā*, *sama*, *nibha*, and *saṃnibha*;
as well as *tulya*, *saṃkāśa*, *nīkāśa*, *prakāśa*, and *pratirūpaka* [are used to denote similarity]. (2.57)
They are opposites, adversaries, antagonists, and contraries;
they are similar, like, concordant, of the same class, and imitative.
Reflected image, counterpart, similar form, equal, and commensurate;
possessing characteristics, resembling, appearing like, having the same side, and compared—these are the similes.

Words such as *kalpadeśīya* and *deśya*, as well as *prakhyā* and *pratinidhi*, the words *savarṇa* and *tulita*, and those that express a meaning that is not inferior [to the original], [are used as substitutes]. (DKD 2.60)
And the compound *bahuvrīhi* in such cases as "moon-faced" (*śaśāṅkavadanā*) rivals, conquers, hates, harms, or roars back [against its object]. (DKD 2.61)
He reviles, despises, treats with contempt, censures, mocks, persecutes, laughs at, envies, and finds fault. (DKd 2.62)
It steals away his good fortune, it robs him of his splendor;
it contends with him and rivals him in comparison.
One places one's foot upon his path, enters into his sphere of activity, follows after him, adheres to him, emulates his conduct, and restrains oneself according to his example. (DK 2.64)
And words such as "it imitates that" indicate similarity;
these are declared in the context of simile (upamā) to provide ease of understanding for poets.
Thus ends the cycle of similes. (DKd 2.65)
A metaphor (*rūpaka*) is said to be a simile in which the distinction [between the object and its attribute] has become concealed;
for example: "the vine-arms," "the lotus-hands," and "the sprout-feet."
Your fingers were the young shoots, the radiance of your nails the flowers;
you, O Goddess of Spring, are our visible presence, with arms like creepers.
Thus, this is called the "uncompounded" (asamasta) compound;
the "smile is the moonlight of the moon-face" is the "compounded-and-uncompounded" (samastavyasta) metaphor.
The lotus of your feet, with its rows of copper-colored petal-like fingers and the filaments of the luster of your nails, is borne upon their heads by kings.

Having superimposed the nature of petals and so forth upon the fingers and so on, and the state of being a lotus upon the foot, by placing these in their appropriate locations, this is a "complete metaphor" (sakalarūpaka).
O passionate one, all of a sudden your face— its sprout-like lower lip quivering—
bears clusters of drops of perspiration with the luster of pearls.

Having turned the water of her virtues into a cluster of blossoms and her lower lip into a sprout, her face here has not been made otherwise; therefore, this is an "Avayavarūpaka" (metaphor of parts).
With dancing eyebrows, dripping drops of perspiration, and blood-red eyes,
this lotus-face reveals her state of intoxication.
Without transforming the facial features themselves, the face alone was made to attain the state of a lotus;
therefore, this is an *avayavirūpaka* (metaphor of the whole).
By your face— with cheeks rosy from intoxication and eyes like red lotuses— this deluded person has been made full of passion.
This is a simile consisting of a single limb; likewise, two or more limbs may also be employed here, where their combination or separation creates a distinction.
"This face, radiant with the flowers of its smile and possessing the bees of its flickering eyes"—
this is a fitting metaphor through the conjunction of flowers and bees.
"This face has the moonlight of a moist smile and the blue lotuses of affectionate eyes"—
this is indeed an improper *rūpaka* (metaphorical identification), because of the incongruity between moonlight and blue lotuses.

Because the whole is transformed while its parts serve as the basis for both transformation and non-transformation, a charming figure known as "the Uneven Metaphor" (*viṣamarūpaka*) arises, as follows: *DKd_2.79*
With your moon-like face, its cheeks flushed with passion and its creeper-like brows dancing, Love is fully capable of crushing the three worlds.
Victorious is the foot of Hari, which has the water of the Daughter of Jahnu clinging to it like a silken garment,
and which serves as the banner for the festival of joy of the gods who are now free from fear of the asuras.
If the form of a banner possessing all its qualifiers is such that it is superimposed upon a foot,
this is a *saviśeṣaṇarūpaka* (metaphor with qualifiers).
It does not close the lotuses, nor does it plunge into the sky;
yet your moon-like face is capable only of stealing away my life-breaths.
Because here the non-performance of the moon's functions and the performance of another function are demonstrated, it is called the "contradictory" metaphor (*viruddha-rūpaka*).
In profundity you are the ocean; in dignity you are the mountain;
and because you grant the desires of the worlds, you are the wish-fulfilling tree.

In this context, by means of reasons such as profundity and so forth, the ocean, the mountain, and the wish-fulfilling tree are treated [as the subject]; thus, this is a "metaphor of the reason" (*heturūpaka*).
"O friend, this lotus-face of yours is worthy of being enjoyed by a royal swan and its fragrance is sought after by bees"— this is a *śliṣṭarūpaka* (a pun-based metaphor).

Just as there are two types of *rūpaka* (metaphor)—namely, those called *upamā* (simile) and *vyatireka* (distinction)—which are based on the perception of similarity or dissimilarity between the secondary and the primary [objects], so too is the desired [figure of speech]. 2.88.
This moon-like face, with its crimson glow from intoxication,
rivals the moon as it rises with the flush of dawn.
The moon is drunk by the gods, but the moon of your face is drunk by me; though that [celestial] moon is never full, its orb is always complete.
"O beautiful one, the moon-nature of your moon-like face, which thus afflicts others, does not correspond [to that of the actual moon]"— this is an *ākṣeparūpaka* (ironic metaphor).
"O fierce one, even your moon-like face burns me mercilessly";
"this is due solely to the fault of my own misfortune"—this is the figure of speech known as *samādhāna-rūpaka* (the metaphorical resolution).
"On this stage of your lotus-face, the dancer of your creeper-like eyebrows performs a graceful dance"— this is a charming "metaphor of metaphors" (rūpakarūpaka).
This is not a face, but this is a lotus; these are not two eyes, but two bees; these are indeed filaments, and not the radiance of your teeth.
By negating the nature of being a face and so forth, and instead representing it as a lotus and so forth,
this is *tattvāpahnavarūpaka* (metaphor by denial of reality), which manifests an excellence of qualities.
There is no end to conceptual constructions regarding forms and similes;
therefore, only a mere indication has been shown by the wise. Let that which was not explicitly stated be inferred.
Thus ends the cycle of metaphors (rūpakacakra). DKd 2.96.
If that which expresses a genus, an action, a quality, or a substance, occurring in a single location, assists the entire sentence, they call that *dīpaka* (the illuminator), as follows: [DK 2.97].
The southern wind sweeps away the withered leaves of the creepers;
that very same wind is capable of shattering the pride of women with drooping limbs.
Your elephants roam in the gardens on the shores of the four oceans, and your virtues, white as kunda flowers, dwell in the groves of the Cakravāla mountains.
The quarters of the sky were darkened by rows of clouds belonging to the rainy season, and the earth was made verdant by delicate streaks of fresh young grass.
By Viṣṇu, as he took his strides, the prosperities of the Dānavas were led away to some unknown place, and from somewhere the divine splendors were brought back.

Thus the *dīpaka* (illuminators) have been explained; likewise, we shall demonstrate some of them occurring at the middle and the end of sentences, as follows: DKD 2.102: Thus the illuminators (*dīpaka*) have been stated; in this same way, we shall show some of them occurring at the middle and the end of sentences as well, for example: [text].
The peacocks dance upon the lap of the *nicula* trees and sing;
they fix their eyes, filled with tears of joy, upon the clouds.
For those away from home, even a gentle breeze becomes pungent, fire becomes like the moon, and the application of sandalwood paste feels like the stroke of a weapon.
The water vomited forth by the clouds, the flock of domestic peacocks,
the flickering garland of lightning, and the power of the flower-bowed god of love.
By you, a blue lotus was placed at your ear; by Smara, his weapon upon his bow;
and by me, my mind was fixed on death—these three things were done simultaneously.

The bright fortnight of the five-arrowed god [Kāma] is for the increase of his white radiance; that fortnight belongs to Passion, and Passion, in turn, belongs to the glory of the festivals of love for the young.

Even though these are instances of *dīpaka* (illumination), because a series of sentences is employed such that each subsequent one depends upon the preceding ones, that is considered *mālādīpaka* (garland-illumination).
The clouds increase the arrogance of the bodiless god of love,
yet they diminish the power of Dharma with their spray tossed up by the wind.
When two contradictory actions are joined here by means of the words "arrogance" (*avalepa*) and "cloud" (*balāhaka*), it is the Illuminator of Contrary Meanings (*tadviruddhārthadīpaka*).
This line of clouds robs the quarters of their expanse, seizes the host of luminaries, and now takes away my very life-breaths. (DK 2.111)
Because multiple words [denoting different subjects] are employed, a single action alone is illuminated here;
since this occurs through a series of clouds, it is therefore called the "Illuminator of a Single Meaning" (ekārthadīpaka).
Carrying fragrant scents, lofty, and possessing a dark luster like the *tamāla* tree,
these clouds wander in the sky, while these elephants roam upon the earth.

Here, because the clouds and the elephants are non-different with respect to their properties, they are connected solely through the act of "wandering"; thus, this is a *śliṣṭārthadīpaka* (an illuminator of double-meaning objects).
In this very manner, the wise should understand the remaining types of *dīpaka* (illuminator) figures as well.
Thus ends the cycle of lamps (dīpakacakra). DKd 2.115.

The repetition of meaning, the repetition of words, and the repetition of both are indeed intended as three distinct ornaments in the very place where the *dīpaka* occurs, as follows: arthāvṛttiḥ padāvṛttir ubhayāvṛttir eva ca | dīpakasthāna eveṣṭam alaṃkāratrayaṃ yathā || DKd 2.116 ||
The kadamba flowers bloom, the kuṭaja trees burst open,
the kandalī plants unfurl, and the kakubha trees blossom.
The garland of clouds causes the flock of peacocks to yearn,
and this god whose banner is a sea-monster causes the minds of young men to yearn as well.
Having conquered the entire world, you now enjoy yourself here with your harem; let your host of enemies, having gone to heaven, enjoy themselves with the Apsarases.
Thus ends the wheel of transmigration. (DKd 2.119)

The expression of negation is an objection (*ākṣepa*), which is threefold in view of the three times; furthermore, it is infinite because the objects of such objections are infinite in variety. (DKD 2.120)
"The bodiless one conquers the universe with five flower-arrows"—this is indeed improbable; yet, the powers of things are truly wondrous.

When the notion of practicing yoga for the conquest of the bodiless god [of love] proceeds here by the force of a cause, yet is subsequently rejected, that is such a case of the "rejection of what has occurred" (vṛttākṣepa). // DKd_2.122 //
"Why do you place a blue lotus on your ear, O sweet-voiced one? Do you think your side-glance is insufficient for this task? (DKD 2.123)
While she was thus interrupting the present moment by placing a blue lotus on her ear, a certain woman was restrained by her lover with these very words of flattery.
I tell you the truth, my dear: you shall not obtain the sight of me with eyes reddened by the lac transferred from the kisses of another.
Thus, this was a pre-emptive anticipation; for she, being exceedingly sensitive, had restrained him with the thought that some offense might perhaps occur from his side in the future.
O slender-limbed one, this softness that has grown upon your limbs is surely false;
for if it were real, why does it cause me such pain so unexpectedly?
This is an instance of the "suggestion of a fact" (dharmākṣepa), wherein the softness of the woman's limbs— already suggested—
is here [negated] by the lover through an action that is contrary to it.
Is she beautiful? This discrimination is not known by whom;
for only a flickering radiance is seen, and not that which is its substratum. (DKD 2.129)
This is an implied negation of the substratum (*dharmyākṣepa*), wherein the substratum is implied by one who,
having already accepted the attribute called "light," intends to speak of its nature as something truly marvelous.
Your eyes are reddened, your sprout-like lower lip quivers, and your eyebrows are arched; yet, even so, I have no fear, for I am without fault.
This is the refutation of the cause: that the Pradhāna is the cause of fear;
for here, one's own fault has been prohibited by a more skillful lover.
That beloved one was far away, yet here comes the arrival of the clouds;
the *nicula* trees are seen in full bloom, and yet I am not dead—what indeed is this?
That is an "implication by effect" (kāryākṣepa), because it precludes the effect—death—by introducing its cause: the arrival of the terrible clouds.
Your journey will not cause me long-lasting distress;
if you must go where you are bound, have no further apprehension on this account.
In this way, by means of a very permission, the course of Kāntā is implied;
since it indicates her death, it is called "the implied denial through permission."
You shall obtain much wealth, and there will be happiness and safety on your path;
nor is there any danger to my life. Nevertheless, my dear one, do not go.
When one who speaks thus of reasons connected to a beloved journey is restrained by her very power, that is called the "suggestion of power."
My hope for life is strong, but my hope for wealth is weak; go or stay, my beloved, but I have made known my own condition.
This is the censure of disregard, which consists of speech uttered with an air of indifference by a woman who is actually in love, intended to stop her beloved from departing.
Go, O beloved, if you must go; may your paths be auspicious.
May my birth also take place in that very place where you have gone.

Thus, this is an instance of the "interruption by words of blessing," wherein the beloved's departure is forbidden by her very indication of her own condition under the guise of offering a benediction.
If your journey is indeed real, let some other [means] be sought by you;
for I am obstructed this very day by Death, who watches for a vulnerability.
Thus, this is the "harsh rebuke" (paruṣākṣepa), because the departure of her beloved is rebuked by one who is overcome with love, preceded by harsh words. (DKD 2.144)
If you are going, go quickly before the sounds emerging from the mouths of your distressed kinsmen—obstacles to your departure—reach your ears. (DKD 2.145)

This is indeed a case of the "suggestion of assistance" (sācivyākṣepa), wherein the departure of her beloved is prohibited by her, who, being exceedingly impassioned, is actually providing assistance for it.
"O my beloved, desiring your welfare, I wish to say 'Go';
yet the words 'Do not go' issue from my mouth—what can I do? (DKd 2.147)
That is the "futility of effort," because it demonstrates the pointlessness of an effort directed toward an undesirable object, since it results in a contrary outcome. (DK 2.148)
Tell me of the departure of that love which grows angry even at the twinkling of an eyelash as a momentary obstacle to its vision; for I desire what is desired by it.
This is an indirect reproach through another, wherein she, being dependent on love,
forbids his journey while hinting at her own purpose.
O Lord, I shall endure separation; grant me the ointment of invisibility, so that when my eyes are anointed, Kandarpa, the striker, may not see me.
"Having proposed a difficult means of livelihood, she now obstructs her husband's departure"— such they call the "objection to a means" (upāyākṣepa).
"O beloved, the words 'I am indeed departing' have already issued from your mouth;
even though they were drawn out by you, what is the use of them now, since my love for you has become faint?"
This is an outburst of anger, by which the beloved’s impending departure is forbidden by one whose self is constrained by overflowing affection and who is overcome with agitation.
A young woman, fainting at the mere sound of her lover’s announcement of his departure, regains consciousness and, upon seeing him, says to her beloved: "Why have you returned so late?"
Thus, when the movement of the beloved is interrupted by a fainting fit arising at that moment,
such is what is called "interruption by fainting" (*mūrchākṣepa*) for the timid-eyed woman.
The blue lotus in the long ponds of your enemies has not been smelled, nor placed upon the ear, nor offered as honey by women; it has simply withered away.
This is a reproach based on compassion; for by demonstrating her pitiable condition, he turns back from the action appropriate [for her] as if out of pity for the lotus.
While this moon of your face exists— whose essence is nectar, which hates the lotuses,
and whose pupils are moist— what need is there for another moon?

Thus, having first set aside the primary moon and then displayed qualities residing in the secondary moon that are similar to them, such a figure is called "the paronomastic rejection" (*śliṣṭākṣepa*).
No wealth whatsoever has been accumulated, no knowledge has been honored, no austerity has been practiced, and my entire life has passed away. (DKD 2.161)

This projection of latent tendencies (anuśaya) is shown here by one whose life has come to an end, because it is demonstrated that after the latent tendencies, there is a turning away from the acquisition of wealth and so forth.
Is this an autumnal cloud, or is it a flock of swans?
That sound heard, resonant with the tinkling of anklets, is not from a rain-cloud.
Thus, this is the removal of doubt;
for by means of that quality so easily attained by the swan, the state of being born from dense clouds is dispelled.
It is a marvel that even though your valor has pervaded the entire universe, it is never satiated;
for when has the insatiable consumer of oblations ever been seen to reach satiety?
This is the "suggestion of another matter" (*arthāntarākṣepa*) which was introduced [in the previous verse] and is here being set aside;
for here, wonder arises from the observation of another matter possessing a quality similar to that [initial subject]. (DKD 2.166)
O Lord of Men, you are never praised with the words "you give," because those who seek wealth take from you what they consider to be their own.
An objection such as this and others like it is known as the "objection regarding the reason" (hetvākṣepa);
by this same method, other varieties [of objections] can also be inferred.
Thus ends the cycle of objections. (DKd 2.168)
Having introduced some matter, the statement of another matter capable of establishing it should be known as *arthāntaranyāsa* (corroboration). (DK 2.169)

Pervading all, yet abiding in particulars; bound by connection, yet possessing contradiction; acting improperly, yet being of a disciplined nature; both appropriate and inappropriate, and the reverse. (DK 2.170)
Such varieties as these have been observed in its practical applications; this series of examples is presented in order to clarify their specific forms.
Behold, even the two blessed ones who are the eyes of the world, the sun and the moon, are going to their setting; by whom can destiny be transgressed?
Clouds indeed remove the fever of embodied beings;
for the great, the very acquisition of their own being is for the sake of allaying the suffering of others.
The Malaya breeze generates joy for the world;
indeed, one endowed with courtesy becomes dear to everyone. (DKD 2.174)
This maker of night brings joy to the world even though he is stained;
for the lord of the twice-born bestows favor upon others even when he is possessed of faults.
Even the sound of bees emerging from throats that have tasted honey becomes harsh to the ears of lovers; such is the nature of sin.
This bed of lotus petals burns my limbs;
indeed, it is only fitting that it be of the nature of burning, as it is a counterpart to fire.
Let the moon wane at will; why does spring distress me? Surely it is improper for the fragrant breeze to perform such a foul deed.
Does even this bed of lotuses exist for the burning of water-lilies? For one who belongs to the sun cannot be gentle toward those who belong to the fierce moon.
Thus ends the cycle of *arthāntaranyāsa* (corroboration by a general truth). // DKd_2.179 //
When a similarity between two things is expressed by words or is implied,
the statement of their difference therein is called *vyatireka* (distinction).
In qualities such as fortitude, beauty, and profundity, you are equal to the ocean; the only difference between you and it is this body of yours.

Thus, this is a single negative concomitance (ekavyatireka), because the difference residing in both [the subject and the example] is brought within the range of cognition by means of a property that resides in only one [the example]. (DKD 2.182)
The ocean has unbroken shores and you are profound;
he resembles collyrium in hue, while you possess the luster of gold.
This is an exclusion of both; for here both qualities that distinguish the two—blackness and tawny-brown—are shown separately.
Both you and the ocean are difficult to restrain, great beings endowed with splendor;
yet this is the difference between you two: he is dull-witted, while you are clever.
Let this very [type] be understood as "with pun" (saśleṣa) because it consists of paronomasia;
furthermore, both the "with objection" (sākṣepa) and the "with reason" (sahetu) are also shown. (DKD 2.186)
Though it is stable, firm, and a treasury of jewels,
the turbid ocean does not even come within your range.
Even though he supports the entire earth with its mountains, islands, and oceans,
Śeṣa is inferior to you because of his status as the bearer of serpents.
This [type of] vyatireka (contrast) is such that it possesses a similarity based on the literal expression;
however, there is also that which possesses a perceived similarity, and that too is now described.
Between these two—your face and the lotus—there is this distinction:
the lotus grows in the water, while your face rests upon you.
The eyes of the deer lack the play of eyebrows and are untouched by the flush of intoxication;
yet this pair of yours is adorned with those very qualities.
In the former [verse], there was merely a statement of distinction; in this one, a further superiority is shown, and yet another similar contrast is demonstrated.
Your face and the lotus are both in full bloom and fragrant;
yet while the lotus has hovering bees, your face has flickering eyes.
This moon is the crest-jewel of the sky; this swan is the ornament of the water;
this sky is garlanded with stars; and this water is filled with blooming white lotuses.

In this [simile], a distinction is made between the sky and water, which possess a perceived similarity in whiteness and so forth, and between the moon and the swan, both of which are recognized as pure. (DKD 2.195)

In the preceding case, there is a similarity with verbal [simile], while in both cases there is a differentiator; the "bee-eyes" and so forth are common to both, as they constitute a dissimilitude based on similarity.
The darkness born of youth obstructs the vision of the young; it cannot be dispelled by the light of jewels, nor can it be removed by the rays of the sun. (DK 2.197)
This is an exclusion by way of similarity: this darkness belongs to the genus of darkness;
it is equal [to other instances] by virtue of obstructing vision, yet it was perceived as distinct from others.
Thus ends the wheel of negative concomitance (vyatirekacakram). (DKd 2.198)
When, by the exclusion of a well-known cause, some other cause or even inherent nature (*svābhāvikatva*) is imagined in a certain case, that is *vibhāvanā*.
The world was enchanting: its geese were neither drunk nor yellowed; the sky was unswept yet stainless; and the water was unpurified yet clear.
O beautiful one, your gaze is dark without being anointed with collyrium; your brow is curved without being bent; and this lower lip of yours is rosy without being stained [with rouge]. (DKD 2.201)
Even if [the state of] intoxication and so forth were produced by drinking and the like, or born from another cause,
or even causeless— since that is what is intended here, there is no contradiction.
The mouth is naturally fragrant, and the body is beautiful without artifice;
yet the moon is an enemy without cause, and Love is a foe without reason.
In this [verse], the cause is directly negated by words such as "by nature" (nisarga), while the result, such as fragrance, is stated; that is *vibhāvanā*.
Thus ends the cycle of the contemplation of the absence of causes. // DKd_2.204 //
Having intended some particular object, the description of another object similar to it—
because it takes the form of a concise expression— is accepted as *samāsokti* (speech of abbreviation).
Behold how the bee, drinking honey at will from a blossoming lotus, kisses even the unopened bud, though it lacks fragrance. (DKD 2.206)
Thus, in this world, the movement of desire is observed in a passionate man who has already engaged in amorous play with mature women, yet still finds interest in some young girl. (DKD 2.207)
Though differing only in their qualificanda, there is one with identical qualifiers,
and there is another with qualifiers that are both different and non-different.
This great tree, with its deeply rooted trunk, constantly nourishing supplicants with its abundance of fruit and providing dense shade— this very one has been reached by me.
By good fortune, I have found this tree, which possesses an extensive spread of branches, is rich in fruit and flowers, lofty, and stable. (2.210)
In both cases, a certain person is described as being a tree;
all the common attributes are present in the former case, whereas in the latter, there are two.
Alas, this ocean, whose waters are naturally sweet and from which the company of serpents has departed, is being dried up by time.
Thus, this is an *apūrva-samāsokti* (novel metaphorical expression), because it indicates the destruction of a man equal to the ocean by means of the cessation of his former attributes.
Thus ends the cycle of *samāsokti* (abbreviated expressions). // DKd_2.213 //
When the intention to express a particularity transcends the limits of worldly experience, that is *atiśayokti* (hyperbole), the highest of poetic ornaments, as for example: [DKD 2.214]
Bearing garlands of jasmine, with fresh sandalwood paste applied to all their limbs, and dressed in linen garments, the women going to meet their lovers were not visible in the moonlight.
The abundance of moonlight has been described as being characterized by excellence; now, something is shown by way of illustration to clarify such things as doubt and intensity.
O beloved, regarding the waist between your breasts and your hips,
the doubt as to whether it exists or not does not cease for me even today.
O lady of shapely hips, it can be determined that you possess a waist, solely because of the impossibility of your heavy breasts remaining in their position otherwise.
"Oh, how vast, O protector of the earth, is the interior of the three worlds, since even the mass of your fame, though impossible to contain, is accommodated within it! (DKD 2.219)
They say that this speech, honored by the Lord of Speech, is the single ultimate resort even for other ornaments; it is called *atiśaya* (superiority).
Thus ends the cycle of hyperboles (atiśayokti). DKd 2.220.

When the mode of being of either a conscious or an unconscious entity exists in one way, yet it is imagined in another way, they know that as *utprekṣā* (poetic fancy), as for example: [text omitted].
Scorched by the midday sun, the elephant plunges into the lake;
I imagine he is intent on uprooting the lotuses that belong to the Sun.

The poet describes the elephant’s plunging into the water as an imaginative conjecture— that it is for the purpose of bathing, drinking, and eating lotus stalks, thereby expiating its enmity toward them.
"This is an ornament for Karna, who is my adversary"—
thinking thus, your eye mostly avoids the lotus on his ear.
The poet describes it by imagining whether or not the blue lotus is touched by the rays of her glance falling from the corners of her eyes.
"Darkness seems to smear my limbs; the sky seems to rain down collyrium"—even this [statement] for the most part lacks the defining characteristics of a poetic conceit (utprekṣā).

In some cases, a misconception arises here due to hearing the word "iva" (like) that there can be no simile with a verb-ending word, thereby transgressing the statement of the authoritative [teacher].
The relationship of standard of comparison and object of comparison depends upon a common attribute; what such attribute can be observed here in the case of "smearing" darkness?
If the act of smearing itself is what is intended, what else could the term "smearer" be?
No one who is not insane would claim that the property and the possessor of the property are one and the same.
If the agent were the object of comparison, it would be subordinated within the verbal expression;
being preoccupied with accomplishing its own action, it would not be capable of depending on anything else.
Even for one who praises [the moon], saying "He who anoints [the earth] is equal to this [darkness]," the claim that "[he anoints] his limbs" is incoherent; such a common quality must also be sought.
Just as in the expression "your face is like the moon," radiance is understood;
so too, from the word *limpati* ("it smears"), nothing other than the act of smearing is understood here.

Therefore, let it be accepted that this verb *limpati* (to smear), having darkness as its agent and the limbs as its object, is here imagined by the person as having the purpose of adhesion. (DK 2.233)
I think, I suspect, certainly, mostly, surely—by such words as these, poetic fancy (utprekṣā) is manifested; the word "as if" (iva) is also of that same nature.
Thus ends the cycle of poetic conceits (utprekṣā). DKd 2.234.
The cause (*hetu*) and the two subtle nuances (*sūkṣmaleśau*) are the supreme ornaments of speech;
the causes are both the productive (*kāraka*) and the indicative (*jñāpaka*), and they are of many kinds, as follows.
This Malaya breeze, which causes the tender shoots of the mature sandalwood trees to sway, produces joy in everyone.
The enhancement here of a form capable of generating delight is designated as an ornament; that [enhancement] is the same even when [the form] has ceased.
Having shaken the sandalwood forest and touched the mountain cascades of Malaya,
this wind has arrived for the destruction of travelers.
For such a wind as this is indeed sufficient to bring about non-existence in a person suffering from the loss of appetite caused by the fever of separation.
In the case of an object to be removed (*nivartya*) or one to be transformed (*vikārya*), its status as a cause is relative to that [action];
however, in the case of an object to be reached (*prāpya*), its causality generally depends solely upon the action.
The cause for that which is to be produced has been shown; now, having provided two examples for the remaining two [types of causes], the indicative cause will be described.
Forests with burgeoning shoots, ponds with blossoming lotuses,
and the full moon— all have been turned into poison for the eyes of the traveler by the God of Love.
Thinking, "I shall make her worthy of honor," the young girl, her eyes askance with a frown of her brows and her lower lip quivering, gazes at her friend who stands in the presence of her beloved.
"The sun has set, the moon shines, and the birds go to their nests"—
even this is quite effective for announcing the state of the time.
"O friend, your mind is clearly afflicted by love— a state that cannot be destroyed by the rays of the moon nor cured by sandalwood water, yet is evident through the heat of your body."
Thus, these charming indicative causes (jñāpaka-hetu) are to be recognized in their applications;
certain captivating non-existence causes (abhāva-hetu) are also being proclaimed.
Through the lack of practice in the sciences, through not associating with the wise,
and through the failure to restrain the senses, calamity arises for men.
The intoxication of talk about desire has passed; the fever of youth has melted away; delusion is destroyed and craving has fallen off; my mind is now fixed upon the holy hermitage.
These are forests, not houses; these are rivers, not women;
these are deer, not kinsmen; therefore my mind rejoices.
That which is utterly non-existent for the noble ones is an unobserved activity;
therefore, all their perfections increase constantly.
The mango blossoms of the garden have not yet burst open;
let a handful of water mixed with sesame seeds be offered to the wives of travelers.
In this context, a real entity— whether in the form of prior non-existence or otherwise—
is the cause for the production of an effect that consists of both existence and non-existence.
The remote cause, that which is innate, likewise that which arises immediately after the action,
and those causes consisting of improper and proper application— thus, the various causes are innumerable.
These [examples] on the paths of preparation (prayogamārga), which rely upon figurative usage (gauṇavṛtti), have been seen to be exceedingly beautiful; their illustrations are as follows.
O lovely lady, that victorious weapon of the bodiless god called your sidelong glance was released elsewhere; by it, even I have been wounded in my heart.
The youth of women, with childhood cast aside,
manifests together with the various delusions of amorous passion in men.
Afterwards, when the orb of the moon has risen and cast its rays abroad,
the ocean of passion in fawn-eyed women has already surged long before.
O Lord, why does the morning glow of the red hue from your two feet cause the lotus-hands of kings to close like buds? (2.258)
The rays of the jasmine-white moons of your toenails are able to cause the lotus-hands of kings to close.
Thus has been shown the nature of such conceptual constructions regarding causes.
Thus is the wheel of causes.
An object that is to be discerned through gestures and physical expressions is known as "subtle" because of its subtlety. (DK 2.260)
Realizing that it was impossible to say to her beloved in the crowded place, "When will our meeting take place?", the frail woman closed her play-lotus.
Here, the closing of the lotus indicates a meeting at night,
intended by her who wished to comfort her beloved afflicted by love.
As her eyes were fixed upon me during that musical gathering, a certain indescribable radiance, tremulous with unrestrained passion, blossomed upon the lotus of her face.
Thus, because its form was not yet manifest, the desire for the festival of love remained established there, having not yet transcended its subtle state.
Thus ends the subtle wheel. (DKd 2.264)
The concealment of the true nature of an object by means of slight hints is [the definition of *leśa*];
its form will become manifest in the example itself.
The guards might discover that I am in love with the princess by the bristling of my hair; alas, this forest is like a cold wind!
"Tears of joy have welled up in me just from seeing this girl;
my eye has been irritated by flower pollen stirred up by the wind. (DKD 2.267)
Thus, this ornament shines most brilliantly when placed in such a context; some, however, understand *leśa* to be either censure or praise expressed only slightly. (DK 2.268)
This young king is virtuous, powerful, and a worthy husband for you;
his mind is attached to the festival of battle even more than to the festival of love.
In this case, praise for the excellence of vigor is indeed a censure intended to turn one away from worldly existence;
it serves for a maiden who desires to enter continuously into the enjoyments [of the world]. (DKD 2.270)
O friend, what is the use of that fickle and merciless man to me?
For he has learned these flattering words only for the sake of wiping away my offense.
Out of passion, she was unable to maintain the pride directed toward her circle of friends; thus, some semblance of a fault was displayed as a virtue—namely, her flattery.
Thus ends the cycle of the fragments. (DKd 2.272)
The subsequent enumeration of the items already mentioned in their proper order is called *yathāsaṃkhya* (enumeration according to number), and it is also termed *krama* (sequence). DKd 2.273.
"O slender one, it is certain that the radiance of your smile, your glance,
and your face has been stolen by the water-lilies, blue lotuses, and lotuses as you entered the water to bathe."
Such is the sequence. (DKd 2.274)

The *preyas* is a narrative that is more dear than the pleasant; the *rasavat* is delicate with aesthetic flavor (*rasa*); and the *ūrjasvin* is that which possesses manifest pride and is endowed with excellence—these three [are the types of *arthālaṃkāra*].
O Govinda, the joy that has arisen within me today because you have come to my home would, in time, be equal to the joy felt again by your very arrival.
Thus Vidura spoke appropriately; such steadfastness could not come from any other source, for Hari is pleased when propitiated by devotion alone. (DKD 2.277)
O Lord, having transcended these forms—Soma, Sūrya, the Maruts, the Earth, the Sky, the Hotṛ priest, Fire, and Water—who are we to behold You? (DKd 2.278)
Thus, when the god was directly perceived, King Rātavarmā’s manifestation of joy should be understood as *preyas* (the more desirable).
"She with whom I intended to be united after death when I resolved upon dying— she,
that very woman of Avanti, has been found by me right here in this very life."

That very affection previously shown has now become *rati*, having attained the state of *śṛṅgāra* (the erotic sentiment) through its association with an abundance of beauty; thus, this speech is imbued with aesthetic flavor (*rasavat*).
He who dragged Kṛṣṇā by her hair while she was before me—this wicked Duḥśāsana has been caught; how can he live for even a moment?
"Having thus reached the highest limit, Krodha attained a fierce nature while Bhīma looked on at his enemy"— this is a speech full of aesthetic flavor (*rasavat*).
Without having conquered the earth bounded by the oceans, without having performed various sacrifices, and without having bestowed wealth upon those who ask for it— how could you be a king?
Thus, this exalted spirit of enthusiasm, abiding in the nature of the heroic sentiment (*vīrarasa*),
is capable of endowing these words with aesthetic flavor (*rasavattva*).
How can that slender-limbed woman, for whom even a bed of flowers causes pain because of her delicate body, lie down upon a funeral pyre filled with fire?
Thus, compassion is remembered as an ornament when it is intensified;
likewise, there are others as well: the loathsome, the comic, the marvelous, and the terrifying.
Drinking again and again the blood of your enemies with their cupped hands,
the flesh-eaters dance together with headless trunks adorned with entrails.
"O friend, this fresh nail-mark upon the slope of your breast, left by one whose pride remains unfaded, must be concealed with your upper garment."
The garments are sprouts, the flowers are necklaces and other ornaments, and the branches are palaces; wonderful indeed are these trees of the Nandana grove!
This is the thunderbolt of Maghavan, with fire residing within its edge;
the mere remembrance of it is sufficient to cause the miscarriage of the embryos of the Daitya women.

In the previous case, sweetness was shown to have its source in the non-vulgarity of the sentence; here, however, the quality of being flavorful in speech is held to depend upon the eight aesthetic sentiments.
Thus ends the chapter on the flavorful [sentiments]. (DKd 2.292)
"Let there be no fear in your heart that 'I am an offender';
my sword never desires to strike those who have turned away from me."
Thus, when an enemy in battle has been released after being restrained by some man possessed of pride,
that [man] should be known as "the powerful" (ūrjasvin) and so forth.
Thus [it is] full of vigor. (DKd 2.294)
When, without directly stating a desired meaning, one describes it by means of another mode of expression for the sake of its very accomplishment, that is recognized as *paryāyokta* (periphrasis).
"That cuckoo is pecking at the blossom of the mango tree;
I shall ward him off, so you two may sit at your ease."
Having brought her friend to the trysting-place with the youth, a certain woman, wishing to bring that festival of love to its conclusion, departed from there.
Thus ends the figure of speech known as *paryāyokta* (indirect expression).
When one who has begun some task achieves its completion through the power of destiny, that they call *samāhita*. (DKD 2.298)
"By good fortune, this thundering of the clouds has arisen for my benefit, as I am about to fall at her feet to dispel her pride."
Thus it is established. (DKD 2.299)
The wise call that figure of speech "the Exalted" (udātta) which consists of the unsurpassed greatness of either intention or power. (DKD 2.300)
That Rāghava, who was undaunted even by the burden of the task of severing the heads of Rāvaṇa, was unable to transgress the command of his guru.
Surrounded by hundreds of reflections cast upon the jeweled walls,
the Lord of Laṅkā was recognized in his true nature by Añjaneya only with great difficulty.
In the former case, the greatness of intention was expressed, while here, the dignity of the exalted rebirth is clearly manifested; thus, both of these have been described as "exalted" (udātta).
Thus ends the section on the acute accent. 2.303.
Apahnuti (concealment) is the perception of something else after having concealed one thing; for example:
"The god of love does not have five arrows; he has a thousand shafts."
Sandalwood, moonlight, gentle breezes, and the southern wind—this creation of mine is composed of fire; it is cool for me, yet hot for others.
Having accepted coolness in others for the sake of his own desire, he reveals heat in himself; thus, this is his denial of the object.
The moon is considered to be so by name because its rays drip with nectar;
yet this [other] entity, whose very nature is its object, is something entirely different, for its rays drip with poison.

Thus, by negating the very nature of the moon in the moon and stating that it possesses the nature of another object due to being afflicted by love, this is considered *svarūpāpahnuti* (concealment of essential nature).

The figure of speech *apahnuti* (concealment), which is based on *upamā* (simile), has already been demonstrated within the section on similes; thus, the detailed expansion of the varieties of *apahnuti* among their respective instances [should be sought] in the illustrative examples.
Thus ends the section on Apahnuti (concealment).
A *śliṣṭa* (paranomasia) is a desired expression that possesses multiple meanings while being endowed with a single form;
it is of two kinds: consisting of non-different words (*abhinnapada*) and consisting mostly of different words (*bhinnapadaprāya*).
Having ascended the eastern mountain, this radiant king with his crimson orb captivates the hearts of the world with his gentle rays.
Why does this unpleasant evening not distress me, as the king— acting like a source of faults while moving along the path of the stars— binds me in such a manner?

The instances of *śleṣa* (paronomasia) that fall within the scope of simile (*upamā*), metaphor (*rūpaka*), objection (*ākṣepa*), contrast (*vyatireka*), and so forth have already been shown; now, some other [instances] are being demonstrated. (DKD 2.313)
There is a conjunction (śleṣa) whose action is non-different, another whose action is non-contradictory, and yet another whose action is contradictory; there is also one that possesses a restriction.
The statement consisting of the rejection of restrictive rules may appear as either non-contradictory or contradictory;
its specific form will become manifest within their very illustrations.
Curved, naturally sweet, and proclaiming an intense passion, the glances sent by beloved women and the female messengers alike draw their lovers toward them.
Sweet, passion-increasing, and tender are the warbling songs of the cuckoos, heard in their intoxicatingly melodious tones; and dark-eyed women are embraced.
Displaying a passion intensified by the consumption of wine, the sun,
the portion of dharma, vanishes, while the god of love (Aṅgaja) expands his power.
In this king alone resides the quality of being sword-like; in his bow alone lies the quality of being curved; and in his arrows alone exists the state of being a seeker.
Thorns exist only on the stalks of lotuses while you provide protection;
or rather, they are seen even upon the embraces of impassioned couples.
That lord was a mountain with many peaks, radiant, ever-rising, skillful,
a protector of subjects, and a wielder of power.
Though Acyuta, he was not the cutter of rain; though a king, he was unaware of decay; though a god, he was not wise; and though Śaṃkara, he was not possessed of serpents.
Thus ends the wheel of paronomasia (śleṣa). (DKd 2.322)
When there is an observation of the deficiency of qualities, genus, actions, and so forth,
for the very purpose of observing a distinction, that is intended as "Poetic Exclusion" (viśeṣokti).
The flower-bowed god’s weapon is neither hard nor sharp;
nevertheless, by it the three worlds were utterly conquered.
She is neither a daughter of the gods nor born from the lineage of the Gandharvas;
nevertheless, she is capable of disrupting even the ascetic penance of the Creator himself.
No frown was knit, nor did his lip quiver, nor did his gaze grow red; yet the host of enemies was conquered.
Neither chariots nor elephants, neither horses nor foot-soldiers [conquer];
by the mere sidelong glance of women, the three worlds are defeated.
Though its wheel is single, its driver is crippled, and its horses are uneven,
the radiant sun nevertheless traverses the vault of the sky.
This very same is the "statement of a specific cause" (hetuviśeṣokti), due to the qualification "he is radiant";
this same sequence applies to the conception of other varieties as well.
Thus ends the cycle of *viśeṣokti* (the figure of speech of specific assertion). // DKd 2.329 //

When something is described by equating it with others possessing superior qualities intended for expression—either for the purpose of praise or censure—that is considered *tulyayogitā* (Equal Pairing). (DKD 2.330)
Yama, Kubera, Varuṇa, the thousand-eyed Indra, and even you yourself bear the title "World-Protector" (Lokapāla), a designation whose scope is not shared by any other.
The unions of fawn-eyed women and the flashes of lightning do not endure for even two moments, even when initiated by the clouds themselves.
Thus ends the figure of speech *tulyayogitā* (Equal Pairing). // DKd_2.332 //
Where there is the observation of the association of contradictory entities, that is considered a contradiction for the very purpose of revealing their specific distinction, as follows: [DK 2.333]
The warbling of the royal swans increases, lovely with passion,
while the cry of the peacocks, its excellence departed, diminishes.
The sky becomes overcast with the clouds of the rainy season,
yet the minds of living beings become once again overcome by passion.
Whom does the body of women—not slender-waisted, broad-hipped, with red lips and dark eyes, with a deep navel and uplifted breasts—not captivate? (DKD 2.336)
O slender one, even your form— with arms like lotus stalks, thighs like plantain trunks, and a face with eyes like lotuses and water lilies— brings us nothing but torment.
The pollen of mango and campaka flowers, stirred up by the garden breeze,
causes the eyes of travelers to well with tears, even though it does not touch them.
O sweet-voiced one, whose eye—though devoted to Kṛṣṇa and Arjuna—is yet hanging down toward Karṇa; how can it be trusted by anyone? (2.339)
Thus, this ornament is perceived in many varieties.
Thus ends the wheel of contradiction (*virodhacakra*).
Aprastutapraśaṃsā (Indirect Praise) is that praise which occurs regarding things not under discussion.
The deer live happily in the forests, serving no one else,
sustained by foods such as grass and sprouts of darbha that are easily obtained without effort.
Thus, this very mode of life of a deer, though irrelevant here, is praised by the high-minded man who is weary of the hardships of serving a king.
Thus ends the figure of speech known as Aprastutapraśaṃsā (Indirect Description).
If one praises while seemingly censuring, that is known as "disguised praise" (vyājastuti);
for in this case, what appear to be defects are actually qualities that find their place there.
This earth, the sustainer of beings, was conquered by Rāma even though he was an ascetic;
it has been conquered by you as well, though you are a king—let there be no pride in you.
"O King, having snatched away the Fortune of the Ancient Man, you now enjoy her; is this fitting for you of the Ikṣvāku lineage?"
The earth, with its serpent-hoods entwined, is your wife;
whence could pride possibly reach its highest peak within you?
Thus, let other varieties of "disguised praise" (vyājastuti) interwoven with paronomasia (śleṣa) be observed; for their detailed expansion is indeed limitless.
Thus ends the figure of speech known as *vyājastuti* (feigned praise).
If something similar to that [object],
whether existent or non-existent, were shown by means of something directed toward a different object, then that might be an illustration (nidarśana).
Rising, this Savitṛ bestows splendor upon the lotuses, in order to manifest the fruit of his powers and his favor toward his friends.
Touched by the rays of the moon, the mass of darkness goes to its defeat,
instantly indicating the miserable end of those who oppose the king.
Thus is the illustration. (DKd 2.350)
Co-utterance (*sahokti*) is the description of qualities and actions by way of their simultaneous occurrence;
whereas the exchange of objects is known as substitution (*parivṛtti*).
Now these nights have grown long along with my sighs,
and those moon-adorned nights have become pale along with my limbs.
The mango blossom grows along with the fainting of travelers,
and the Malaya breezes fall away together with their very lives.
The days of spring grow in splendor along with the joys of people, accompanied by forest breezes fragrant with scent and made delightful by the warbling of cuckoos.
Thus, some examples of *sahokti* (conjoined expression) have been provided here.
Thus ends the discussion of Sahokti;
now, some illustration of the form of Parivṛtti (Exchange) is provided.
By your arm, as it delivered a blow with a weapon, the long-earned fame of those kings— pale as a white water-lily— was snatched away from them.
Thus ends the section on exchange. DKd 2.356.
Blessing (āśis) is the expression of a wish for a desired object, as in:
"May the supreme light, which is beyond the reach of speech and mind, protect you."
Thus is the benediction. (DKd 2.357)
The defects of lack of correspondence (ananvaya) and doubt (saṃdeha) have been shown only in the context of similes (upamā);
likewise, the figure of simile-metaphor (upamārūpaka) has also been shown only in the context of metaphors (rūpaka).
This is indeed a variety of *utprekṣā*, as well as a part of *utprekṣā*;
however, the commingling of various ornaments is called *saṃsṛṣṭi*.
The existence of a relationship between primary and subordinate elements, or the equality of all elements;
these are the two ways in which the blending of figures of speech (alaṃkārasaṃsṛṣṭi) is to be characterized.
O charming girl, the lotuses challenge the beauty of your face;
for what is difficult for those who possess both calyx and stalk?
Darkness seems to smear my limbs; the sky seems to rain down collyrium;
and my vision has become fruitless, like service rendered to a wicked man.
Pun (śleṣa) generally nourishes the beauty of all forms of figurative expression (vakrokti);
for the entire domain of speech is divided into two parts: the description of things as they are (svabhāvokti) and figurative expression (vakrokti).
Thus ends the section on combination. // DKd 2.363 //
They call that "bhāvika," a quality pertaining to the composition; *bhāva* is the poet's intention, which remains present throughout the poems until their completion. (DKD 2.364)
The mutual dependence of all things, objects, stages, specific qualities, and even useless actions; and the description of their locations.
The manifestation of even a profound subject matter occurs through the power of the sequence of expression;
since all this depends upon the internal state [of the poet], they know it as *bhāvika*.
Thus ends the section on the future (bhāvika). DKd 2.366.

And whatever has been described in other scriptures regarding the characteristics of the junctures (*saṃdhi*), the dramatic elements (*vṛttyaṅga*), and so forth— that too is accepted by us as nothing other than ornamentation (*alaṅkāra*).
This very path has been opened by means of a measured treatment, having condensed the infinite expansion of poetic ornaments;
for it is practice alone that is capable of revealing the specific distinctions that transcend the range of words as they revolve.
Thus ends the second chapter, titled "The Classification of Figures of Sense," in the *Kāvyādarśa* composed by Ācārya Daṇḍin.
